Penalized Regression: Ridge and LASSO¶

So far we have approached feature selection---that is, selection of which ${\bf X}$ variables to based our predictions on---by considering several subsets of features and comparing scores. But what if we want to consider all of the features? We don't necessarily want to select all the features to include in our model, because we run the risk of overfitting to the training data. But maybe we want to consider every feature for selection rather than just a few subsets. Penalized regression is one way of performing de facto feature selection: throw all the available features into the model and let the model fitting sort out which to include.

In [1]:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.compose import make_column_selector, ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder, PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, Ridge, Lasso, ElasticNet
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score

We'll use the Ames housing data. We'll do a little cleaning first to:

  • Drop a few columns that have mostly missing values
  • Drop a few rows with missing values
  • Drop the ID columns (row order and PID)
In [2]:
ames = pd.read_csv("AmesHousing.txt", sep="\t")

# Get rid of columns with mostly NaN values
good_cols = ames.isna().sum() < 100
ames = ames.loc[:,good_cols]

# Drop other NAs
ames = ames.dropna()

# drop ID columns and put target in y
X = ames.drop(["SalePrice", "Order", "PID"], axis = 1)
y = ames["SalePrice"]

Let's try a linear regression model first. We'll standardize numerical predictors and dummify categorical predictors.

In [4]:
ct = ColumnTransformer(
  [
    ("dummify",
    OneHotEncoder(sparse_output = False, handle_unknown='ignore'),
    make_column_selector(dtype_include=object)),
    ("standardize",
    StandardScaler(),
    make_column_selector(dtype_include=np.number))
  ],
  remainder = "passthrough"
).set_output(transform="pandas")
In [5]:
lr_pipeline = Pipeline(
  [("preprocessing", ct),
  ("linear_regression", LinearRegression())]
)
In [6]:
lr_pipeline.fit(X, y)

Parameters
steps steps: list of tuples

List of (name of step, estimator) tuples that are to be chained in
sequential order. To be compatible with the scikit-learn API, all steps
must define `fit`. All non-last steps must also define `transform`. See
:ref:`Combining Estimators ` for more details. 		[('preprocessing', ...), ('linear_regression', ...)]
transform_input transform_input: list of str, default=None

The names of the :term:`metadata` parameters that should be transformed by the
pipeline before passing it to the step consuming it.

This enables transforming some input arguments to ``fit`` (other than ``X``)
to be transformed by the steps of the pipeline up to the step which requires
them. Requirement is defined via :ref:`metadata routing `.
For instance, this can be used to pass a validation set through the pipeline.

You can only set this if metadata routing is enabled, which you
can enable using ``sklearn.set_config(enable_metadata_routing=True)``.

.. versionadded:: 1.6 		None
memory memory: str or object with the joblib.Memory interface, default=None

Used to cache the fitted transformers of the pipeline. The last step
will never be cached, even if it is a transformer. By default, no
caching is performed. If a string is given, it is the path to the
caching directory. Enabling caching triggers a clone of the transformers
before fitting. Therefore, the transformer instance given to the
pipeline cannot be inspected directly. Use the attribute ``named_steps``
or ``steps`` to inspect estimators within the pipeline. Caching the
transformers is advantageous when fitting is time consuming. See
:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_neighbors_plot_caching_nearest_neighbors.py`
for an example on how to enable caching. 		None
verbose verbose: bool, default=False

If True, the time elapsed while fitting each step will be printed as it
is completed. 		False
Parameters
transformers transformers: list of tuples

List of (name, transformer, columns) tuples specifying the
transformer objects to be applied to subsets of the data.

name : str
Like in Pipeline and FeatureUnion, this allows the transformer and
its parameters to be set using ``set_params`` and searched in grid
search.
transformer : {'drop', 'passthrough'} or estimator
Estimator must support :term:`fit` and :term:`transform`.
Special-cased strings 'drop' and 'passthrough' are accepted as
well, to indicate to drop the columns or to pass them through
untransformed, respectively.
columns : str, array-like of str, int, array-like of int, array-like of bool, slice or callable
Indexes the data on its second axis. Integers are interpreted as
positional columns, while strings can reference DataFrame columns
by name. A scalar string or int should be used where
``transformer`` expects X to be a 1d array-like (vector),
otherwise a 2d array will be passed to the transformer.
A callable is passed the input data `X` and can return any of the
above. To select multiple columns by name or dtype, you can use
:obj:`make_column_selector`. 		[('dummify', ...), ('standardize', ...)]
remainder remainder: {'drop', 'passthrough'} or estimator, default='drop'

By default, only the specified columns in `transformers` are
transformed and combined in the output, and the non-specified
columns are dropped. (default of ``'drop'``).
By specifying ``remainder='passthrough'``, all remaining columns that
were not specified in `transformers`, but present in the data passed
to `fit` will be automatically passed through. This subset of columns
is concatenated with the output of the transformers. For dataframes,
extra columns not seen during `fit` will be excluded from the output
of `transform`.
By setting ``remainder`` to be an estimator, the remaining
non-specified columns will use the ``remainder`` estimator. The
estimator must support :term:`fit` and :term:`transform`.
Note that using this feature requires that the DataFrame columns
input at :term:`fit` and :term:`transform` have identical order. 		'passthrough'
sparse_threshold sparse_threshold: float, default=0.3

If the output of the different transformers contains sparse matrices,
these will be stacked as a sparse matrix if the overall density is
lower than this value. Use ``sparse_threshold=0`` to always return
dense. When the transformed output consists of all dense data, the
stacked result will be dense, and this keyword will be ignored. 		0.3
n_jobs n_jobs: int, default=None

Number of jobs to run in parallel.
``None`` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context.
``-1`` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary `
for more details. 		None
transformer_weights transformer_weights: dict, default=None

Multiplicative weights for features per transformer. The output of the
transformer is multiplied by these weights. Keys are transformer names,
values the weights. 		None
verbose verbose: bool, default=False

If True, the time elapsed while fitting each transformer will be
printed as it is completed. 		False
verbose_feature_names_out verbose_feature_names_out: bool, str or Callable[[str, str], str], default=True

- If True, :meth:`ColumnTransformer.get_feature_names_out` will prefix
all feature names with the name of the transformer that generated that
feature. It is equivalent to setting
`verbose_feature_names_out="{transformer_name}__{feature_name}"`.
- If False, :meth:`ColumnTransformer.get_feature_names_out` will not
prefix any feature names and will error if feature names are not
unique.
- If ``Callable[[str, str], str]``,
:meth:`ColumnTransformer.get_feature_names_out` will rename all the features
using the name of the transformer. The first argument of the callable is the
transformer name and the second argument is the feature name. The returned
string will be the new feature name.
- If ``str``, it must be a string ready for formatting. The given string will
be formatted using two field names: ``transformer_name`` and ``feature_name``.
e.g. ``"{feature_name}__{transformer_name}"``. See :meth:`str.format` method
from the standard library for more info.

.. versionadded:: 1.0

`verbose_feature_names_out` can be a callable or a string to be formatted. 		True

This parameter has no effect.

.. note::
If you do not access the list of columns for the remainder columns

<sklearn.compose._column_transformer.make_column_selector object at 0x7fbdc6f6be00>
Parameters
categories categories: 'auto' or a list of array-like, default='auto'

Categories (unique values) per feature:

- 'auto' : Determine categories automatically from the training data.
- list : ``categories[i]`` holds the categories expected in the ith
column. The passed categories should not mix strings and numeric
values within a single feature, and should be sorted in case of
numeric values.

The used categories can be found in the ``categories_`` attribute.

.. versionadded:: 0.20 		'auto'
drop drop: {'first', 'if_binary'} or an array-like of shape (n_features,), default=None

Specifies a methodology to use to drop one of the categories per
feature. This is useful in situations where perfectly collinear
features cause problems, such as when feeding the resulting data
into an unregularized linear regression model.

However, dropping one category breaks the symmetry of the original
representation and can therefore induce a bias in downstream models,
for instance for penalized linear classification or regression models.

- None : retain all features (the default).
- 'first' : drop the first category in each feature. If only one
category is present, the feature will be dropped entirely.
- 'if_binary' : drop the first category in each feature with two
categories. Features with 1 or more than 2 categories are
left intact.
- array : ``drop[i]`` is the category in feature ``X[:, i]`` that
should be dropped.

When `max_categories` or `min_frequency` is configured to group
infrequent categories, the dropping behavior is handled after the
grouping.

.. versionadded:: 0.21
The parameter `drop` was added in 0.21.

.. versionchanged:: 0.23
The option `drop='if_binary'` was added in 0.23.

.. versionchanged:: 1.1
Support for dropping infrequent categories. 		None
sparse_output sparse_output: bool, default=True

When ``True``, it returns a :class:`scipy.sparse.csr_matrix`,
i.e. a sparse matrix in "Compressed Sparse Row" (CSR) format.

.. versionadded:: 1.2
`sparse` was renamed to `sparse_output` 		False
dtype dtype: number type, default=np.float64

Desired dtype of output. 		<class 'numpy.float64'>
handle_unknown handle_unknown: {'error', 'ignore', 'infrequent_if_exist', 'warn'}, default='error'

Specifies the way unknown categories are handled during :meth:`transform`.

- 'error' : Raise an error if an unknown category is present during transform.
- 'ignore' : When an unknown category is encountered during
transform, the resulting one-hot encoded columns for this feature
will be all zeros. In the inverse transform, an unknown category
will be denoted as None.
- 'infrequent_if_exist' : When an unknown category is encountered
during transform, the resulting one-hot encoded columns for this
feature will map to the infrequent category if it exists. The
infrequent category will be mapped to the last position in the
encoding. During inverse transform, an unknown category will be
mapped to the category denoted `'infrequent'` if it exists. If the
`'infrequent'` category does not exist, then :meth:`transform` and
:meth:`inverse_transform` will handle an unknown category as with
`handle_unknown='ignore'`. Infrequent categories exist based on
`min_frequency` and `max_categories`. Read more in the
:ref:`User Guide `.
- 'warn' : When an unknown category is encountered during transform
a warning is issued, and the encoding then proceeds as described for
`handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist"`.

.. versionchanged:: 1.1
`'infrequent_if_exist'` was added to automatically handle unknown
categories and infrequent categories.

.. versionadded:: 1.6
The option `"warn"` was added in 1.6. 		'ignore'
min_frequency min_frequency: int or float, default=None

Specifies the minimum frequency below which a category will be
considered infrequent.

- If `int`, categories with a smaller cardinality will be considered
infrequent.

- If `float`, categories with a smaller cardinality than
`min_frequency * n_samples` will be considered infrequent.

.. versionadded:: 1.1
Read more in the :ref:`User Guide `. 		None
max_categories max_categories: int, default=None

Specifies an upper limit to the number of output features for each input
feature when considering infrequent categories. If there are infrequent
categories, `max_categories` includes the category representing the
infrequent categories along with the frequent categories. If `None`,
there is no limit to the number of output features.

.. versionadded:: 1.1
Read more in the :ref:`User Guide `. 		None
feature_name_combiner feature_name_combiner: "concat" or callable, default="concat"

Callable with signature `def callable(input_feature, category)` that returns a
string. This is used to create feature names to be returned by
:meth:`get_feature_names_out`.

`"concat"` concatenates encoded feature name and category with
`feature + "_" + str(category)`.E.g. feature X with values 1, 6, 7 create
feature names `X_1, X_6, X_7`.

.. versionadded:: 1.3 		'concat'

copy copy: bool, default=True

If False, try to avoid a copy and do inplace scaling instead.
This is not guaranteed to always work inplace; e.g. if the data is
not a NumPy array or scipy.sparse CSR matrix, a copy may still be
returned. 		True
with_mean with_mean: bool, default=True

If True, center the data before scaling.
This does not work (and will raise an exception) when attempted on
sparse matrices, because centering them entails building a dense
matrix which in common use cases is likely to be too large to fit in

Parameters
fit_intercept fit_intercept: bool, default=True

Whether to calculate the intercept for this model. If set

copy_X copy_X: bool, default=True

If True, X will be copied; else, it may be overwritten. 		True
tol tol: float, default=1e-6

The precision of the solution (`coef_`) is determined by `tol` which
specifies a different convergence criterion for the `lsqr` solver.
`tol` is set as `atol` and `btol` of :func:`scipy.sparse.linalg.lsqr` when

.. versionadded:: 1.7 		1e-06
n_jobs n_jobs: int, default=None

The number of jobs to use for the computation. This will only provide
speedup in case of sufficiently large problems, that is if firstly

:obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context. ``-1`` means using all

positive positive: bool, default=False

When set to ``True``, forces the coefficients to be positive. This

For a comparison between a linear regression model with positive constraints

Now let's use cross-validation to evaluate based on $R^2$.

In [7]:
cross_val_score(lr_pipeline, X, y, cv = 10, scoring = 'r2')
Out[7]:
array([0.88433686, 0.90316706, 0.87507511, 0.91216037, 0.82269502,
       0.73890838, 0.86879893, 0.63798647, 0.90277443, 0.90350125])

Hmmm... linear regression on all the predictors does not seem as bad as the textbook suggests, though there is considerably variability between the scores based on the different folds.

Let's add second degree polynomial terms for all numerical predictors and see what happens.

In [8]:
numeric_poly = Pipeline([
    ("polynomial_features", PolynomialFeatures(degree=2)),
    ("standardize", StandardScaler())
])

ct_poly = ColumnTransformer(
    [
        ("dummify",
         OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False, handle_unknown="ignore"),
         make_column_selector(dtype_include=object)),

        ("numeric_poly",
         numeric_poly,
         ["Gr Liv Area", "Overall Qual", "Year Built", "Total Bsmt SF", "Garage Area", "Full Bath", "Lot Area", "Overall Cond"])
    ],
    remainder="drop"
).set_output(transform="pandas")
In [9]:
poly_pipeline = Pipeline(
  [("preprocessing", ct_poly),
  ("linear_regression", LinearRegression())]
)
In [10]:
poly_pipeline.fit(X, y)

categories categories: 'auto' or a list of array-like, default='auto'

drop drop: {'first', 'if_binary'} or an array-like of shape (n_features,), default=None

Specifies a methodology to use to drop one of the categories per
feature. This is useful in situations where perfectly collinear
features cause problems, such as when feeding the resulting data
into an unregularized linear regression model.

However, dropping one category breaks the symmetry of the original
representation and can therefore induce a bias in downstream models,
for instance for penalized linear classification or regression models.

array([0.86536599, 0.88750621, 0.56271095])

OK, now that's bad. The moral is that just throwing in all the predictors might fit the training data well but can be pretty terrible when it comes to making predictions for new observations. We want to be more selective without having to laboriously search through many possible subsets of predictors. With 67 predictors there are $2^{67}\approx 10^{20}$ possible subsets---even before we consider polynomial terms, interactions, transformations, etc---so it would be impossible to fit every possible subset.

Instead, we include all predictors but "penalize" variables that don't contribute much to the model. Before getting to the penalty we'll consider some motivating conceptual questions.

  1. Consider a simple linear regression of sale price on a single variable like living area. What is the process by which the coefficient for living area is determined? How does "least squares" work? DISCUSS

Answer: Ordinary least squares chooses the intercept and living-area slope to minimize the sum of squared residuals, $\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2$. Each residual is actual sale price minus predicted sale price; squaring penalizes larger misses.

  1. Now consider a multiple of regression on living area and number of bedrooms, without standardizing variables. How does least squares work in this case? DISCUSS

Answer: Least squares simultaneously chooses the intercept, living-area coefficient, and bedroom coefficient to minimize the same sum of squared errors, $\sum_i[y_i-(\beta_0+\beta_1\text{Area}_i+\beta_2\text{Bedrooms}_i)]^2$. Each slope measures its variable while holding the other predictor constant.

  1. If you fit the linear model, without standarizing variables, how do you interpret the coefficients for living area and number of bedrooms? What is their rough order of magnitude? Can we determine directly from the coefficients which variable the predicted prices are more sensitive to? DISCUSS

Answer: Without scaling, living area has a slope measured in dollars per extra square foot and bedrooms in dollars per additional bedroom, holding the other fixed. The square-foot slope may be tens or hundreds of dollars per square foot, while the bedroom coefficient may be thousands or tens of thousands of dollars per bedroom (and either sign is possible after controlling for area). Raw coefficient magnitudes are not directly comparable, because one unit of area is not comparable to one bedroom. These are illustrative orders of magnitude, not coefficients estimated here.

  1. If you standardize the variables first, how would you interpret the model coefficients? How could you determine, roughly, which variable the predicted prices are more sensitive to? DISCUSS

Answer: If the predictors have mean zero and standard deviation one, each coefficient represents the predicted dollar change in sale price for a one-standard-deviation increase in that predictor, holding the others fixed. Larger absolute standardized slopes usually imply greater sensitivity to a typical change in a feature (although correlation among features complicates interpretation).

  1. If we want to make the predictions less sensitive to a particular standardized variable, what in principle should we do to its coefficient? DISCUSS

Answer: Reduce the absolute magnitude of its coefficient toward zero; then a given change in that standardized predictor changes predictions by less.

  1. If we want to make the predictions not at all sensitive to a particular standardized variable, what in principle should we do to its coefficient? DISCUSS

Answer: Set its coefficient exactly to zero. The fitted prediction no longer depends directly on that predictor.

  1. Why does including a penalty like in ridge regression or LASSO "shrink" coefficients towards 0? DISCUSS

Answer: Ridge and LASSO minimize prediction error plus a positive penalty on coefficient magnitudes. Increasing a coefficient can improve fit but costs penalty; the optimum often trades some in-sample fit for smaller coefficients. Ridge uses squared coefficients ($L_2$); LASSO uses absolute values ($L_1$).

  1. Why is it important to standarize variables when using a penalty? DISCUSS

Answer: Without standardization, the numerical scale and units of a predictor determine the size of its fitted coefficient. A common penalty would therefore penalize the same predictive effect differently across variables. Scaling numerical predictors to comparable units makes regularization more equitable. Binary/dummy predictors may be treated differently depending on the modeling goal.

  1. What happens if the penalty parameter $\lambda$ is 0? DISCUSS

Answer: With $\lambda=0$ (called alpha=0 in scikit-learn), the penalty vanishes, giving the ordinary least squares objective. Use LinearRegression rather than a penalized estimator with alpha=0.

  1. What happens as the penalty parameter $\lambda$ gets larger and larger? DISCUSS

Answer: Stronger penalties push slopes toward zero. Ridge slopes approach zero smoothly; LASSO can set some exactly to zero. With an extremely strong penalty, predictions approach the fitted intercept (approximately the training response mean if predictors are centered).

  1. Why do we not penalize the intercept? DISCUSS

Answer: The intercept sets the baseline level of the response and does not measure sensitivity to an explanatory variable. Penalizing it would improperly force the baseline predicted sale price toward zero; the slopes should receive the penalty instead.

  1. Assume $\lambda = 1$. Suppose a standardized predictor has a small coefficient, say $\beta = 0.1$. How much does that coefficient add to the LASSO penalty versus the ridge penalty? If the coefficient were reduced from 0.1 to 0, how much would each penalty decrease? Which penalty offers a larger payoff for eliminating a small coefficient entirely? DISCUSS

Answer: At $\lambda=1$ and $\beta=0.1$, the LASSO penalty contribution is $|0.1|=0.1$, while the ridge contribution is $(0.1)^2=0.01$ (using the convention that the penalty is $\lambda\sum|\beta_j|$ or $\lambda\sum\beta_j^2$). Shrinking that coefficient to zero saves 0.1 for LASSO versus 0.01 for ridge. LASSO gives a larger payoff for eliminating a small nonzero coefficient. Note that implementations may use a constant scaling factor.

  • Ridge regression shrinks all coefficient estimates toward zero but typically keeps every predictor in the model.
  • LASSO regression shrinks coefficients and can set some exactly to zero, automatically removing those predictors.
  • Choose ridge when predictors are highly correlated and you think many of them contain useful predictive information. Ridge tends to share influence among correlated variables.
  • Choose LASSO when you want a simpler, more interpretable model with automatic variable selection.
  • With highly correlated predictors, LASSO may keep one and drop the others—sometimes somewhat arbitrarily—while ridge usually retains all of them with smaller coefficients.
  • Both methods are useful when there are many predictors or when ordinary least squares may overfit.

Note that in scikit-learn the penalty parameter $\lambda$ is called alpha.

Ridge Regression¶

Let's fit regression regression first.

  [("preprocessing", ct),
  ("ridge_regression", Ridge(alpha=1))]
)

specifies a different convergence criterion for each solver:

- 'svd': `tol` has no impact.

- 'cholesky': `tol` has no impact.

- 'sparse_cg': norm of residuals smaller than `tol`.

solver solver: {'auto', 'svd', 'cholesky', 'lsqr', 'sparse_cg', 'sag', 'saga', 'lbfgs'}, default='auto'

Solver to use in the computational routines:

- 'auto' chooses the solver automatically based on the type of data.

- 'svd' uses a Singular Value Decomposition of X to compute the Ridge
coefficients. It is the most stable solver, in particular more stable
for singular matrices than 'cholesky' at the cost of being slower.

- 'cholesky' uses the standard :func:`scipy.linalg.solve` function to
obtain a closed-form solution.

- 'sparse_cg' uses the conjugate gradient solver as found in
:func:`scipy.sparse.linalg.cg`. As an iterative algorithm, this solver is
more appropriate than 'cholesky' for large-scale data
(possibility to set `tol` and `max_iter`).

- 'lsqr' uses the dedicated regularized least-squares routine
:func:`scipy.sparse.linalg.lsqr`. It is the fastest and uses an iterative
procedure.

- 'sag' uses a Stochastic Average Gradient descent, and 'saga' uses
its improved, unbiased version named SAGA. Both methods also use an
iterative procedure, and are often faster than other solvers when
both n_samples and n_features are large. Note that 'sag' and
'saga' fast convergence is only guaranteed on features with
approximately the same scale. You can preprocess the data with a
scaler from :mod:`sklearn.preprocessing`.

- 'lbfgs' uses L-BFGS-B algorithm implemented in
:func:`scipy.optimize.minimize`. It can be used only when `positive`
is True.

All solvers except 'svd' support both dense and sparse data. However, only
'lsqr', 'sag', 'sparse_cg', and 'lbfgs' support sparse input when
`fit_intercept` is True.

coef_compare["ridge"] = ridge_pipeline.named_steps['ridge_regression'].coef_
coef_compare["diff"] = abs(coef_compare["lr"]) - abs(coef_compare["ridge"])

Parameters
steps steps: list of tuples

List of (name of step, estimator) tuples that are to be chained in

must define `fit`. All non-last steps must also define `transform`. See

transform_input transform_input: list of str, default=None

The names of the :term:`metadata` parameters that should be transformed by the
pipeline before passing it to the step consuming it.

This enables transforming some input arguments to ``fit`` (other than ``X``)
to be transformed by the steps of the pipeline up to the step which requires
them. Requirement is defined via :ref:`metadata routing `.
For instance, this can be used to pass a validation set through the pipeline.

You can only set this if metadata routing is enabled, which you
can enable using ``sklearn.set_config(enable_metadata_routing=True)``.

Used to cache the fitted transformers of the pipeline. The last step

caching directory. Enabling caching triggers a clone of the transformers
before fitting. Therefore, the transformer instance given to the
pipeline cannot be inspected directly. Use the attribute ``named_steps``
or ``steps`` to inspect estimators within the pipeline. Caching the
transformers is advantageous when fitting is time consuming. See
:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_neighbors_plot_caching_nearest_neighbors.py`
for an example on how to enable caching. 		None

Parameters
transformers transformers: list of tuples

List of (name, transformer, columns) tuples specifying the
transformer objects to be applied to subsets of the data.

name : str
Like in Pipeline and FeatureUnion, this allows the transformer and
its parameters to be set using ``set_params`` and searched in grid
search.
transformer : {'drop', 'passthrough'} or estimator
Estimator must support :term:`fit` and :term:`transform`.
Special-cased strings 'drop' and 'passthrough' are accepted as
well, to indicate to drop the columns or to pass them through
untransformed, respectively.
columns : str, array-like of str, int, array-like of int, array-like of bool, slice or callable
Indexes the data on its second axis. Integers are interpreted as
positional columns, while strings can reference DataFrame columns
by name. A scalar string or int should be used where
``transformer`` expects X to be a 1d array-like (vector),
otherwise a 2d array will be passed to the transformer.
A callable is passed the input data `X` and can return any of the
above. To select multiple columns by name or dtype, you can use
:obj:`make_column_selector`. 		[('dummify', ...), ('numeric_poly', ...)]
remainder remainder: {'drop', 'passthrough'} or estimator, default='drop'

By default, only the specified columns in `transformers` are
transformed and combined in the output, and the non-specified
columns are dropped. (default of ``'drop'``).
By specifying ``remainder='passthrough'``, all remaining columns that
were not specified in `transformers`, but present in the data passed
to `fit` will be automatically passed through. This subset of columns
is concatenated with the output of the transformers. For dataframes,
extra columns not seen during `fit` will be excluded from the output
of `transform`.
By setting ``remainder`` to be an estimator, the remaining
non-specified columns will use the ``remainder`` estimator. The
estimator must support :term:`fit` and :term:`transform`.
Note that using this feature requires that the DataFrame columns
input at :term:`fit` and :term:`transform` have identical order. 		'drop'

Parameters
categories categories: 'auto' or a list of array-like, default='auto'

Categories (unique values) per feature:

- 'auto' : Determine categories automatically from the training data.
- list : ``categories[i]`` holds the categories expected in the ith
column. The passed categories should not mix strings and numeric
values within a single feature, and should be sorted in case of
numeric values.

The used categories can be found in the ``categories_`` attribute.

.. versionadded:: 0.20 		'auto'
drop drop: {'first', 'if_binary'} or an array-like of shape (n_features,), default=None

Specifies a methodology to use to drop one of the categories per
feature. This is useful in situations where perfectly collinear
features cause problems, such as when feeding the resulting data
into an unregularized linear regression model.

However, dropping one category breaks the symmetry of the original
representation and can therefore induce a bias in downstream models,
for instance for penalized linear classification or regression models.

- None : retain all features (the default).
- 'first' : drop the first category in each feature. If only one
category is present, the feature will be dropped entirely.
- 'if_binary' : drop the first category in each feature with two
categories. Features with 1 or more than 2 categories are
left intact.
- array : ``drop[i]`` is the category in feature ``X[:, i]`` that
should be dropped.

When `max_categories` or `min_frequency` is configured to group
infrequent categories, the dropping behavior is handled after the
grouping.

.. versionadded:: 0.21
The parameter `drop` was added in 0.21.

.. versionchanged:: 0.23
The option `drop='if_binary'` was added in 0.23.

Support for dropping infrequent categories. 		None

handle_unknown handle_unknown: {'error', 'ignore', 'infrequent_if_exist', 'warn'}, default='error'

Specifies the way unknown categories are handled during :meth:`transform`.

- 'error' : Raise an error if an unknown category is present during transform.
- 'ignore' : When an unknown category is encountered during
transform, the resulting one-hot encoded columns for this feature
will be all zeros. In the inverse transform, an unknown category
will be denoted as None.
- 'infrequent_if_exist' : When an unknown category is encountered
during transform, the resulting one-hot encoded columns for this
feature will map to the infrequent category if it exists. The
infrequent category will be mapped to the last position in the
encoding. During inverse transform, an unknown category will be
mapped to the category denoted `'infrequent'` if it exists. If the
`'infrequent'` category does not exist, then :meth:`transform` and
:meth:`inverse_transform` will handle an unknown category as with
`handle_unknown='ignore'`. Infrequent categories exist based on
`min_frequency` and `max_categories`. Read more in the
:ref:`User Guide `.
- 'warn' : When an unknown category is encountered during transform
a warning is issued, and the encoding then proceeds as described for
`handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist"`.

poly_coef_compare["ridge_poly"] = ridge_poly_pipeline.named_steps["ridge_regression"].coef_

poly_coef_compare["diff_poly"] = (
    poly_coef_compare["lr_poly"].abs()
    - poly_coef_compare["ridge_poly"].abs()
)

name : str

transformer : {'drop', 'passthrough'} or estimator

untransformed, respectively.
columns : str, array-like of str, int, array-like of int, array-like of bool, slice or callable
Indexes the data on its second axis. Integers are interpreted as
positional columns, while strings can reference DataFrame columns
by name. A scalar string or int should be used where
``transformer`` expects X to be a 1d array-like (vector),
otherwise a 2d array will be passed to the transformer.

above. To select multiple columns by name or dtype, you can use

remainder remainder: {'drop', 'passthrough'} or estimator, default='drop'

columns are dropped. (default of ``'drop'``).
By specifying ``remainder='passthrough'``, all remaining columns that
were not specified in `transformers`, but present in the data passed
to `fit` will be automatically passed through. This subset of columns
is concatenated with the output of the transformers. For dataframes,
extra columns not seen during `fit` will be excluded from the output
of `transform`.
By setting ``remainder`` to be an estimator, the remaining
non-specified columns will use the ``remainder`` estimator. The
estimator must support :term:`fit` and :term:`transform`.
Note that using this feature requires that the DataFrame columns
input at :term:`fit` and :term:`transform` have identical order. 		'passthrough'

Parameters
categories categories: 'auto' or a list of array-like, default='auto'

Categories (unique values) per feature:

- 'auto' : Determine categories automatically from the training data.
- list : ``categories[i]`` holds the categories expected in the ith
column. The passed categories should not mix strings and numeric
values within a single feature, and should be sorted in case of
numeric values.

The used categories can be found in the ``categories_`` attribute.

.. versionadded:: 0.20 		'auto'
drop drop: {'first', 'if_binary'} or an array-like of shape (n_features,), default=None

Specifies a methodology to use to drop one of the categories per
feature. This is useful in situations where perfectly collinear
features cause problems, such as when feeding the resulting data
into an unregularized linear regression model.

However, dropping one category breaks the symmetry of the original
representation and can therefore induce a bias in downstream models,
for instance for penalized linear classification or regression models.

- None : retain all features (the default).
- 'first' : drop the first category in each feature. If only one
category is present, the feature will be dropped entirely.
- 'if_binary' : drop the first category in each feature with two
categories. Features with 1 or more than 2 categories are
left intact.
- array : ``drop[i]`` is the category in feature ``X[:, i]`` that
should be dropped.

When `max_categories` or `min_frequency` is configured to group
infrequent categories, the dropping behavior is handled after the
grouping.

.. versionadded:: 0.21
The parameter `drop` was added in 0.21.

.. versionchanged:: 0.23
The option `drop='if_binary'` was added in 0.23.

.. versionchanged:: 1.1
Support for dropping infrequent categories. 		None
sparse_output sparse_output: bool, default=True

When ``True``, it returns a :class:`scipy.sparse.csr_matrix`,
i.e. a sparse matrix in "Compressed Sparse Row" (CSR) format.

.. versionadded:: 1.2
`sparse` was renamed to `sparse_output` 		False
dtype dtype: number type, default=np.float64

Desired dtype of output. 		<class 'numpy.float64'>
handle_unknown handle_unknown: {'error', 'ignore', 'infrequent_if_exist', 'warn'}, default='error'

Specifies the way unknown categories are handled during :meth:`transform`.

- 'error' : Raise an error if an unknown category is present during transform.
- 'ignore' : When an unknown category is encountered during
transform, the resulting one-hot encoded columns for this feature
will be all zeros. In the inverse transform, an unknown category
will be denoted as None.
- 'infrequent_if_exist' : When an unknown category is encountered
during transform, the resulting one-hot encoded columns for this
feature will map to the infrequent category if it exists. The
infrequent category will be mapped to the last position in the
encoding. During inverse transform, an unknown category will be
mapped to the category denoted `'infrequent'` if it exists. If the
`'infrequent'` category does not exist, then :meth:`transform` and
:meth:`inverse_transform` will handle an unknown category as with
`handle_unknown='ignore'`. Infrequent categories exist based on
`min_frequency` and `max_categories`. Read more in the
:ref:`User Guide `.
- 'warn' : When an unknown category is encountered during transform
a warning is issued, and the encoding then proceeds as described for
`handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist"`.

.. versionchanged:: 1.1
`'infrequent_if_exist'` was added to automatically handle unknown
categories and infrequent categories.

.. versionadded:: 1.6
The option `"warn"` was added in 1.6. 		'ignore'
min_frequency min_frequency: int or float, default=None

Specifies the minimum frequency below which a category will be
considered infrequent.

- If `int`, categories with a smaller cardinality will be considered
infrequent.

- If `float`, categories with a smaller cardinality than
`min_frequency * n_samples` will be considered infrequent.

.. versionadded:: 1.1
Read more in the :ref:`User Guide `. 		None
max_categories max_categories: int, default=None

Specifies an upper limit to the number of output features for each input
feature when considering infrequent categories. If there are infrequent
categories, `max_categories` includes the category representing the
infrequent categories along with the frequent categories. If `None`,
there is no limit to the number of output features.

.. versionadded:: 1.1
Read more in the :ref:`User Guide `. 		None
feature_name_combiner feature_name_combiner: "concat" or callable, default="concat"

Callable with signature `def callable(input_feature, category)` that returns a
string. This is used to create feature names to be returned by
:meth:`get_feature_names_out`.

`"concat"` concatenates encoded feature name and category with
`feature + "_" + str(category)`.E.g. feature X with values 1, 6, 7 create
feature names `X_1, X_6, X_7`.

.. versionadded:: 1.3 		'concat'

Parameters
copy copy: bool, default=True

If False, try to avoid a copy and do inplace scaling instead.
This is not guaranteed to always work inplace; e.g. if the data is
not a NumPy array or scipy.sparse CSR matrix, a copy may still be
returned. 		True
with_mean with_mean: bool, default=True

If True, center the data before scaling.
This does not work (and will raise an exception) when attempted on
sparse matrices, because centering them entails building a dense
matrix which in common use cases is likely to be too large to fit in

with_std with_std: bool, default=True

If True, scale the data to unit variance (or equivalently,
unit standard deviation). 		True 
[]
passthrough
Parameters
alpha alpha: float, default=1.0

Constant that multiplies the L1 term, controlling regularization
strength. `alpha` must be a non-negative float i.e. in `[0, inf)`.

When `alpha = 0`, the objective is equivalent to ordinary least
squares, solved by the :class:`LinearRegression` object. For numerical
reasons, using `alpha = 0` with the `Lasso` object is not advised.
Instead, you should use the :class:`LinearRegression` object. 		10
fit_intercept fit_intercept: bool, default=True

Whether to calculate the intercept for this model. If set
to False, no intercept will be used in calculations
(i.e. data is expected to be centered). 		True
precompute precompute: bool or array-like of shape (n_features, n_features), default=False

Whether to use a precomputed Gram matrix to speed up
calculations. The Gram matrix can also be passed as argument.
For sparse input this option is always ``False`` to preserve sparsity. 		False
copy_X copy_X: bool, default=True

If ``True``, X will be copied; else, it may be overwritten. 		True
max_iter max_iter: int, default=1000

The maximum number of iterations. 		10000
tol tol: float, default=1e-4

The tolerance for the optimization: if the updates are smaller or equal to
``tol``, the optimization code checks the dual gap for optimality and continues
until it is smaller or equal to ``tol``, see Notes below. 		0.0001
warm_start warm_start: bool, default=False

When set to ``True``, reuse the solution of the previous call to fit as
initialization, otherwise, just erase the previous solution.
See :term:`the Glossary `. 		False
positive positive: bool, default=False

When set to ``True``, forces the coefficients to be positive. 		False
random_state random_state: int, RandomState instance, default=None

The seed of the pseudo random number generator that selects a random
feature to update. Used when ``selection`` == 'random'.
Pass an int for reproducible output across multiple function calls.
See :term:`Glossary `. 		None
selection selection: {'cyclic', 'random'}, default='cyclic'

If set to 'random', a random coefficient is updated every iteration
rather than looping over features sequentially by default. This
(setting to 'random') often leads to significantly faster convergence
especially when tol is higher than 1e-4. 		'cyclic'

The used categories can be found in the ``categories_`` attribute.

.. versionadded:: 0.20 		'auto'
drop drop: {'first', 'if_binary'} or an array-like of shape (n_features,), default=None

Specifies a methodology to use to drop one of the categories per
feature. This is useful in situations where perfectly collinear
features cause problems, such as when feeding the resulting data
into an unregularized linear regression model.

However, dropping one category breaks the symmetry of the original
representation and can therefore induce a bias in downstream models,
for instance for penalized linear classification or regression models.

- None : retain all features (the default).
- 'first' : drop the first category in each feature. If only one
category is present, the feature will be dropped entirely.
- 'if_binary' : drop the first category in each feature with two
categories. Features with 1 or more than 2 categories are
left intact.
- array : ``drop[i]`` is the category in feature ``X[:, i]`` that
should be dropped.

When `max_categories` or `min_frequency` is configured to group
infrequent categories, the dropping behavior is handled after the
grouping.

.. versionadded:: 0.21
The parameter `drop` was added in 0.21.

.. versionchanged:: 0.23
The option `drop='if_binary'` was added in 0.23.

.. versionchanged:: 1.1
Support for dropping infrequent categories. 		None
sparse_output sparse_output: bool, default=True

When ``True``, it returns a :class:`scipy.sparse.csr_matrix`,
i.e. a sparse matrix in "Compressed Sparse Row" (CSR) format.

.. versionadded:: 1.2
`sparse` was renamed to `sparse_output` 		False
dtype dtype: number type, default=np.float64

Desired dtype of output. 		<class 'numpy.float64'>
handle_unknown handle_unknown: {'error', 'ignore', 'infrequent_if_exist', 'warn'}, default='error'

Specifies the way unknown categories are handled during :meth:`transform`.

- 'error' : Raise an error if an unknown category is present during transform.
- 'ignore' : When an unknown category is encountered during
transform, the resulting one-hot encoded columns for this feature
will be all zeros. In the inverse transform, an unknown category
will be denoted as None.
- 'infrequent_if_exist' : When an unknown category is encountered
during transform, the resulting one-hot encoded columns for this
feature will map to the infrequent category if it exists. The
infrequent category will be mapped to the last position in the
encoding. During inverse transform, an unknown category will be
mapped to the category denoted `'infrequent'` if it exists. If the
`'infrequent'` category does not exist, then :meth:`transform` and
:meth:`inverse_transform` will handle an unknown category as with
`handle_unknown='ignore'`. Infrequent categories exist based on
`min_frequency` and `max_categories`. Read more in the
:ref:`User Guide `.
- 'warn' : When an unknown category is encountered during transform
a warning is issued, and the encoding then proceeds as described for
`handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist"`.

.. versionchanged:: 1.1
`'infrequent_if_exist'` was added to automatically handle unknown
categories and infrequent categories.

.. versionadded:: 1.6
The option `"warn"` was added in 1.6. 		'ignore'

Specifies the minimum frequency below which a category will be
considered infrequent.

- If `int`, categories with a smaller cardinality will be considered
infrequent.

- If `float`, categories with a smaller cardinality than
`min_frequency * n_samples` will be considered infrequent.

.. versionadded:: 1.1
Read more in the :ref:`User Guide `. 		None

Specifies an upper limit to the number of output features for each input

Parameters
degree degree: int or tuple (min_degree, max_degree), default=2

If a single int is given, it specifies the maximal degree of the
polynomial features. If a tuple `(min_degree, max_degree)` is passed,
then `min_degree` is the minimum and `max_degree` is the maximum
polynomial degree of the generated features. Note that `min_degree=0`
and `min_degree=1` are equivalent as outputting the degree zero term is
determined by `include_bias`. 		2
interaction_only interaction_only: bool, default=False

If `True`, only interaction features are produced: features that are
products of at most `degree` *distinct* input features, i.e. terms with
power of 2 or higher of the same input feature are excluded:

- included: `x[0]`, `x[1]`, `x[0] * x[1]`, etc.
- excluded: `x[0] ** 2`, `x[0] ** 2 * x[1]`, etc. 		False
include_bias include_bias: bool, default=True

If `True` (default), then include a bias column, the feature in which
all polynomial powers are zero (i.e. a column of ones - acts as an
intercept term in a linear model). 		True
order order: {'C', 'F'}, default='C'

Order of output array in the dense case. `'F'` order is faster to
compute, but may slow down subsequent estimators.

.. versionadded:: 0.21 		'C'
Parameters
copy copy: bool, default=True

If False, try to avoid a copy and do inplace scaling instead.
This is not guaranteed to always work inplace; e.g. if the data is
not a NumPy array or scipy.sparse CSR matrix, a copy may still be
returned. 		True
with_mean with_mean: bool, default=True

If True, center the data before scaling.
This does not work (and will raise an exception) when attempted on
sparse matrices, because centering them entails building a dense
matrix which in common use cases is likely to be too large to fit in

with_std with_std: bool, default=True

If True, scale the data to unit variance (or equivalently,

Parameters
alpha alpha: float, default=1.0

Constant that multiplies the L1 term, controlling regularization
strength. `alpha` must be a non-negative float i.e. in `[0, inf)`.

When `alpha = 0`, the objective is equivalent to ordinary least
squares, solved by the :class:`LinearRegression` object. For numerical
reasons, using `alpha = 0` with the `Lasso` object is not advised.
Instead, you should use the :class:`LinearRegression` object. 		10
fit_intercept fit_intercept: bool, default=True

Whether to calculate the intercept for this model. If set
to False, no intercept will be used in calculations

Whether to use a precomputed Gram matrix to speed up

copy_X copy_X: bool, default=True

If ``True``, X will be copied; else, it may be overwritten. 		True
max_iter max_iter: int, default=1000

The maximum number of iterations. 		10000
tol tol: float, default=1e-4

The tolerance for the optimization: if the updates are smaller or equal to

When set to ``True``, reuse the solution of the previous call to fit as

See :term:`the Glossary `. 		False
positive positive: bool, default=False

When set to ``True``, forces the coefficients to be positive. 		False
random_state random_state: int, RandomState instance, default=None

The seed of the pseudo random number generator that selects a random
feature to update. Used when ``selection`` == 'random'.
Pass an int for reproducible output across multiple function calls.

If set to 'random', a random coefficient is updated every iteration

Grid search on alpha parameter¶

Note that useful values of alpha to consider depend on the scale of the $y$ variable.

In [36]:
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

lasso_pipeline = Pipeline(
  [("preprocessing", ct),
  ("lasso_regression", Lasso(alpha = 1, max_iter=10000))]
).set_output(transform="pandas")

alphas = {'lasso_regression__alpha': np.array([10000, 1000, 100, 10, 1])}

gscv = GridSearchCV(lasso_pipeline, param_grid=alphas, cv = 5, scoring='r2')
In [37]:
gscv_fitted = gscv.fit(X, y)

Elastic Net¶

  • Elastic net combines ridge and LASSO penalties, so it both shrinks coefficients and can set some coefficients exactly to zero.
  • It is often preferred when you want variable selection but also have strongly correlated predictors.
  • Unlike LASSO, elastic net tends to keep correlated predictors together rather than choosing one and discarding the others.
  • It has two tuning choices: the overall penalty strength and the balance between ridge-like shrinkage and LASSO-like variable selection.
  • Think of it as a middle ground: ridge keeps all predictors, LASSO selects a sparse subset, and elastic net can select groups of useful predictors while dropping clearly unhelpful ones.
In [39]:
elastic_pipeline = Pipeline(
  [("preprocessing", ct),
  ("elastic_net", ElasticNet(alpha=1, l1_ratio=0.5, max_iter=10000))]
)
In [40]:
cross_val_score(elastic_pipeline, X, y, cv = 10, scoring = 'r2')

Parameters
steps steps: list of tuples

List of (name of step, estimator) tuples that are to be chained in
sequential order. To be compatible with the scikit-learn API, all steps
must define `fit`. All non-last steps must also define `transform`. See
:ref:`Combining Estimators ` for more details. 		[('preprocessing', ...), ('elastic_net', ...)]
transform_input transform_input: list of str, default=None

The names of the :term:`metadata` parameters that should be transformed by the
pipeline before passing it to the step consuming it.

This enables transforming some input arguments to ``fit`` (other than ``X``)
to be transformed by the steps of the pipeline up to the step which requires
them. Requirement is defined via :ref:`metadata routing `.
For instance, this can be used to pass a validation set through the pipeline.

You can only set this if metadata routing is enabled, which you
can enable using ``sklearn.set_config(enable_metadata_routing=True)``.

.. versionadded:: 1.6 		None
memory memory: str or object with the joblib.Memory interface, default=None

Used to cache the fitted transformers of the pipeline. The last step
will never be cached, even if it is a transformer. By default, no
caching is performed. If a string is given, it is the path to the
caching directory. Enabling caching triggers a clone of the transformers
before fitting. Therefore, the transformer instance given to the
pipeline cannot be inspected directly. Use the attribute ``named_steps``
or ``steps`` to inspect estimators within the pipeline. Caching the
transformers is advantageous when fitting is time consuming. See
:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_neighbors_plot_caching_nearest_neighbors.py`
for an example on how to enable caching. 		None

If True, the time elapsed while fitting each step will be printed as it

transformers transformers: list of tuples

List of (name, transformer, columns) tuples specifying the

name : str
Like in Pipeline and FeatureUnion, this allows the transformer and

transformer : {'drop', 'passthrough'} or estimator
Estimator must support :term:`fit` and :term:`transform`.
Special-cased strings 'drop' and 'passthrough' are accepted as

columns : str, array-like of str, int, array-like of int, array-like of bool, slice or callable
Indexes the data on its second axis. Integers are interpreted as
positional columns, while strings can reference DataFrame columns
by name. A scalar string or int should be used where
``transformer`` expects X to be a 1d array-like (vector),
otherwise a 2d array will be passed to the transformer.
A callable is passed the input data `X` and can return any of the
above. To select multiple columns by name or dtype, you can use

remainder remainder: {'drop', 'passthrough'} or estimator, default='drop'

By default, only the specified columns in `transformers` are
transformed and combined in the output, and the non-specified
columns are dropped. (default of ``'drop'``).
By specifying ``remainder='passthrough'``, all remaining columns that
were not specified in `transformers`, but present in the data passed
to `fit` will be automatically passed through. This subset of columns
is concatenated with the output of the transformers. For dataframes,
extra columns not seen during `fit` will be excluded from the output
of `transform`.
By setting ``remainder`` to be an estimator, the remaining
non-specified columns will use the ``remainder`` estimator. The
estimator must support :term:`fit` and :term:`transform`.
Note that using this feature requires that the DataFrame columns
input at :term:`fit` and :term:`transform` have identical order. 		'passthrough'

.. versionadded:: 1.1
Read more in the :ref:`User Guide `. 		None
max_categories max_categories: int, default=None

Specifies an upper limit to the number of output features for each input
feature when considering infrequent categories. If there are infrequent
categories, `max_categories` includes the category representing the
infrequent categories along with the frequent categories. If `None`,
there is no limit to the number of output features.

.. versionadded:: 1.1
Read more in the :ref:`User Guide `. 		None
feature_name_combiner feature_name_combiner: "concat" or callable, default="concat"

Callable with signature `def callable(input_feature, category)` that returns a
string. This is used to create feature names to be returned by
:meth:`get_feature_names_out`.

`"concat"` concatenates encoded feature name and category with
`feature + "_" + str(category)`.E.g. feature X with values 1, 6, 7 create
feature names `X_1, X_6, X_7`.

Parameters
alpha alpha: float, default=1.0

Constant that multiplies the penalty terms. Defaults to 1.0.
See the notes for the exact mathematical meaning of this
parameter. ``alpha = 0`` is equivalent to an ordinary least square,
solved by the :class:`LinearRegression` object. For numerical
reasons, using ``alpha = 0`` with the ``Lasso`` object is not advised.
Given this, you should use the :class:`LinearRegression` object. 		1
l1_ratio l1_ratio: float, default=0.5

The ElasticNet mixing parameter, with ``0 <= l1_ratio <= 1``. For
``l1_ratio = 0`` the penalty is an L2 penalty. ``For l1_ratio = 1`` it
is an L1 penalty. For ``0 < l1_ratio < 1``, the penalty is a
combination of L1 and L2. 		0.5
fit_intercept fit_intercept: bool, default=True

Whether the intercept should be estimated or not. If ``False``, the
data is assumed to be already centered. 		True

Whether to use a precomputed Gram matrix to speed up
calculations. The Gram matrix can also be passed as argument.
For sparse input this option is always ``False`` to preserve sparsity.

The tolerance for the optimization: if the updates are smaller or equal to

When set to ``True``, reuse the solution of the previous call to fit as

Practice Activity¶

Loans Data¶

The loans data set represents thousands of loans made through the Lending Club platform, which is a platform that allows individuals to lend to other individuals. Of course, not all loans are created equal. Someone who is a essentially a sure bet to pay back a loan will have an easier time getting a loan with a low interest rate than someone who appears to be riskier. And for people who are very risky? They may not even get a loan offer, or they may not have accepted the loan offer due to a high interest rate. It is important to keep that last part in mind, since this dataset only represents loans actually made, i.e. do not mistake this data for loan applications!

Some information about the data set is here. There are also some related exercises in this OpenIntro textbook.

Our goal will be to develop a regression model for predicting interest_rate.

We will have a competition to see who can come up with the model with the smallest test RMSE. Fit several models and try to find the smallest test RMSE. When you think you have a good one, share your model and its test RMSE. Then see what other people have done; can you do even better?

Previously you considered selected subsets of features. Now you should try, Ridge, LASSO, and elastic net.

You should use GridSearchCV to tune at least one parameter.

Note: you should do some exploration of the data first before you start fitting models.

Practice Activity: Lending Club model competition¶

Goal: Predict interest_rate for held-out loans and report test-set RMSE. Compare ordinary linear regression, ridge, LASSO, and Elastic Net; use cross-validation to tune regularization. Only predictors plausibly known at the time of loan application are used. In particular, grade, sub_grade, installment, and post-origination repayment/status variables are excluded to avoid target-related leakage.

In [50]:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, GridSearchCV
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, Ridge, Lasso, ElasticNet

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
df["interest_rate"].hist(bins=35, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set(title="Loan interest-rate distribution", xlabel="Interest rate (%)", ylabel="Loans")
df.boxplot(column="interest_rate", by="term", ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set(title="Interest rate by loan term", xlabel="Term (months)", ylabel="Interest rate (%)")
plt.suptitle("")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
In [51]:
# These are application-time variables, not grade, interest-dependent payments, or loan outcomes.
numeric_features = [
    "annual_income", "debt_to_income", "loan_amount", "term", "emp_length",
    "delinq_2y", "inquiries_last_12m", "total_credit_lines",
    "open_credit_lines", "total_credit_limit", "total_credit_utilized",
    "num_historical_failed_to_pay", "accounts_opened_24m",
    "account_never_delinq_percent", "public_record_bankrupt"
]
categorical_features = ["homeownership", "verified_income", "loan_purpose", "application_type"]
features = numeric_features + categorical_features
X_loans = df[features].copy()
y_loans = df["interest_rate"].copy()
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X_loans, y_loans, test_size=0.20, random_state=42
)
num_steps = Pipeline([
    ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
    ("scale", StandardScaler())
])
cat_steps = Pipeline([
    ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
    ("encode", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False))
])
preprocess_loans = ColumnTransformer([
    ("numeric", num_steps, numeric_features),
    ("categorical", cat_steps, categorical_features)
])
print("Training rows:", len(X_train), "Test rows:", len(X_test))
print("Predictor counts:", len(numeric_features), "numeric;", len(categorical_features), "categorical")

Training rows: 8000 Test rows: 2000
Predictor counts: 15 numeric; 4 categorical
In [52]:
# Tune penalties using only the training set. Higher CV score = lower RMSE.
candidates = {
    "Linear regression": (LinearRegression(), {}),
    "Ridge": (Ridge(), {"model__alpha": [1, 10, 100, 1000]}),
    "LASSO": (Lasso(max_iter=10000), {"model__alpha": [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10]}),
    "Elastic Net": (ElasticNet(max_iter=10000), {
        "model__alpha": [0.01, 0.1, 1],
        "model__l1_ratio": [0.2, 0.5, 0.8]
    })
}
fits = {}
results = []
for name, (estimator, grid) in candidates.items():
    pipe = Pipeline([("prep", preprocess_loans), ("model", estimator)])
    search = GridSearchCV(
        pipe, param_grid=grid, cv=3,
        scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error", n_jobs=1
    )
    search.fit(X_train, y_train)
    fits[name] = search
    results.append({"Model": name,
                    "CV RMSE (rate points)": -search.best_score_,
                    "Tuned parameters": search.best_params_})
cv_table = pd.DataFrame(results).sort_values("CV RMSE (rate points)")
print("Three-fold cross-validation comparison (training set only):")
print(cv_table.to_string(index=False))

# One held-out test comparison after model choice. RMSE is in percentage points.
test_rows = []
for name, search in fits.items():
    preds = search.predict(X_test)
    test_rows.append({"Model": name,
                      "Test RMSE (rate points)": np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, preds)),
                      "Test R2": r2_score(y_test, preds)})
test_table = pd.DataFrame(test_rows).sort_values("Test RMSE (rate points)")
display(test_table.round(4))
cv_winner = cv_table.iloc[0]["Model"]
print("Selected by cross-validation:", cv_winner)
print("Selected model's held-out test RMSE:", round(test_table.set_index("Model").loc[cv_winner, "Test RMSE (rate points)"], 4), "percentage points")
pred = fits[cv_winner].predict(X_test)
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 5))
plt.scatter(y_test, pred, alpha=.24, s=11)
lims = [min(y_test.min(), pred.min()), max(y_test.max(), pred.max())]
plt.plot(lims, lims, "k--", lw=1)
plt.xlabel("Actual interest rate (%)")
plt.ylabel("Predicted interest rate (%)")
plt.title(f"Held-out test predictions: {cv_winner}")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
Model Test RMSE (rate points) Test R2
1 Ridge 4.3032 0.3016
3 Elastic Net 4.3038 0.3014
2 LASSO 4.3044 0.3012
0 Linear regression 4.3107 0.2991 
Selected by cross-validation: Elastic Net
Selected model's held-out test RMSE: 4.3038 percentage points

Interpretation: Compare the cross-validated RMSE across all candidates, select the model with the smallest CV RMSE, and use its held-out test RMSE as an estimate of predictive performance on unseen loans. Interest rates are expressed in percent, so an RMSE of 3 means roughly 3 percentage points, not 3% of the interest rate. The held-out test set is not used during tuning. Because these are originated loans, the model does not automatically generalize to rejected applications.
